summary: Defines a Telnet option that disables the exchange of go-ahead signals between the Telnet modules. It is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: The Telnet Suppress Go Ahead option lets the two ends agree that they do not need Go Ahead signals between data. Each direction is negotiated separately, and the default is to send the signals.

questions: what is telnet suppress go ahead
what is the telnet suppress go ahead option
subtitle: Lets Telnet peers agree to omit Go Ahead signals on one or both data directions.

tldr.problem: A full-duplex terminal and host may not need the Go Ahead signal that belongs to Telnet's nominal half-duplex model.
tldr.mechanism: The SUPPRESS-GO-AHEAD option lets each direction independently negotiate whether the sender may omit Go Ahead signals.
tldr.outcome: When the option is active, senders need not transmit Go Ahead and should send characters with minimal buffering, subject to other agreements.

today: RFC 858 is listed as an Internet Standard in the unit metadata. The metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why Suppress Go Ahead
sections.content:
The Network Virtual Terminal assumes a half-duplex style of communication that uses a Go Ahead signal. A full-duplex terminal and a host designed for full-duplex use may not need this signal.

This option lets the parties agree that one end, the other end, or both ends can stop sending Go Ahead signals with their data.
sections.plainLanguage: Some connections can send data both ways without taking turns. The option lets them stop sending a signal that is unnecessary for that arrangement.

sections.title: Negotiating the Option
sections.content:
The option is named SUPPRESS-GO-AHEAD and has code 3. WILL and DO request or confirm suppression, while WON'T and DON'T require Go Ahead signals to continue.

The default is that both ends send Go Ahead signals. Suppression applies separately to each direction, even if the peers usually enable it in both.
sections.plainLanguage: The peers negotiate whether each sender can omit Go Ahead signals. Unless they agree to suppression, Go Ahead signals continue to be sent.

sections.title: Sending Data After Agreement
sections.content:
When suppression is active, the sender does not need to transmit Go Ahead signals. A received Go Ahead command should then be treated as a no-operation, though it should not normally be sent in this mode.

Because suppression is similar to line-at-a-time mode in reverse, a sender should try to transmit characters as soon as possible, with minimal buffering, while respecting other agreements.
sections.plainLanguage: Once suppression is active, data can flow without Go Ahead signals. The sender should avoid holding characters in buffers longer than necessary.

sections.title: Working with Echo
sections.content: The RFC notes that implementations may couple Suppress Go Ahead with the Echo option. Both options will normally need to be active to provide what users commonly understand as character-at-a-time remote echoing.
sections.plainLanguage: Remote echoing one character at a time usually needs both this option and ECHO. Each controls a different part of the interactive exchange.
